evidence_fragments.content:
How Far Are Surgeons from Surgical World Models?
A Pilot Study on Zero-shot Surgical Video Generation with Expert Assessment
Zhen Chen†1,Qing Xu 2,Jinlin Wu 3,Biao Yang †4,Yuhao Zhai †5,Geng Guo 4,Jing Zhang 5,Yinlu Ding 5,
Nassir Navab6,Jiebo Luo 7

It comprises 50 video clips sourced from six
independent recordings of laparoscopic hysterectomy [30] and endoscopic pituitary surgery [31], covering a
diverse range of procedural stages and complexities to ensure a representative testbed. Using this benchmark,
we task the Veo-3 model [10] with generating 8-second video continuations from a single input frame under
two prompting conditions: a baseline prompt and a stage-aware prompt.

We introduce theSurgVeobenchmark, the first publicly available benchmark specifically designed for evaluating
the world modeling capabilities of video generation models in surgical contexts.

A starting surgical frame and a text prompt are fed into the Veo model
to generate an 8-second surgical video prediction. This output is then scored by expert surgeons by comparing it to
the real 8-second reference video with a focus on four dimensions of surgical plausibility, particularly at the 1-second,
3-second, and 8-second time points.

To ensure data diversity and representativeness, we source full-length, high-definition surgical video recordings
from established public datasets. For the laparoscopic surgery track, we collect 3 independent laparoscopic
hysterectomy surgeries from the AutoLaparo dataset [30] with the resolution of1, 920 × 1, 080at 25 frames-
per-second (fps). For the neurosurgery track, we adopt 3 independent endoscopic pituitary surgeries from the
PitVis dataset [31] with the resolution of1,280×720at 24 fps.

Specifically, the laparoscopic surgery track in Fig. 7(a) contains 18 video segments, while the
neurosurgery track in Fig. 7(a) includes 32 video segments. Please note that not all surgeries include every
stage, reflecting the variability in surgical workflows.

This track features video clips from microscopic cranial procedures, characterized
by high magnification microscopic views, extremely delicate tissue handling of neural and vascular
structures, and specialized neurosurgical instrumentation.

The core task of this study is to evaluate the zero-shot surgical video generation of the advanced video
generation models. The Veo-3 model is adopted without any fine-tuning on surgical video data, and is tasked
to generate a logically coherent and surgically plausible 8-second video continuation based solely on the input
frame and a text prompt.

1. Baseline Prompt: Provide only the procedure type (e.g., "This is a laparoscopic hysterectomy") and
general requirements for visual quality and anatomical realism. This condition tests whether the model
can autonomously infer appropriate next steps from visual context alone.
2. Stage-aware Prompt: In addition to baseline information, we further specify the current surgical stage
explicitly (e.g., "The current stage is vessel ligation"). This condition tests whether providing explicit
contextual knowledge improves the surgical plausibility of the generated video.

The evaluation is conducted by a panel of four board-certified surgeons with extensive clinical experience.
To ensure domain-specific expertise, two laparoscopic surgeons independently evaluate the laparoscopic
hysterectomy videos of the laparoscopic surgery track, and two neurosurgeons independently evaluate the
endoscopic pituitary surgery videos of the neurosurgery track.

For the evaluation, surgeons use the 8-second real surgical video as a professional reference to understand the
context and what a correct surgical progression entails. With this reference in mind, they then independently
score the 8-second generated video, providing scores on a 5-point integer scale (1 = Very Poor; 5 = Indis-
tinguishable from Reality) at three specific temporal checkpoints: 1-second, 3-second, and 8-second. This
temporal evaluation structure allows for tracking the degradation or maintenance of plausibility over the
prediction horizon.

• Visual quality distortions: The generated video exhibits a sudden, unnatural increase in brightness,
inconsistent with stable surgical lighting conditions.
•Surgical instrument errors: The model hallucinates a non-existent, fabricated instrument, whereas the
real procedure uses a standard scalpel.
• Inappropriate surgical operations: The generated video shows the dissector moving to the right, which
is procedurally incorrect for the scene; the real operation requires a leftward movement.
• Inappropriate surgical targets: The model depicts an instrument manipulating mucus, while the correct
procedure involves a coordinated action of irrigation and suction on a different target.
• Environment feedback errors: The model violates physical laws by showing a suction tool pulling an
entire block of gel-foam as if it is a solid, attached mass, rather than suctioning loose fluid and debris
from its surface.
• Surgical intent errors: The real procedure involves injecting biologic glue onto the dura, but the model
incorrectly predicts a completely different intent,i.e., wiping the dura with a cotton patty.

In both procedures, the four most dominant error categories are surgical intent errors (21.9% in
laparoscopic surgery, 22.0% in neurosurgery), environment feedback errors (17.2% in laparoscopic surgery,
22.0% in neurosurgery), surgical instrument errors (17.2% in laparoscopic surgery, 17.7% in neurosurgery),
and inappropriate surgical operations (15.6% in laparoscopic surgery, 21.3% in neurosurgery).

Such a model could
revolutionize medical education by providing trainees with interactive, high-fidelity simulators for procedural
practice. It could also enhance patient safety by enabling pre-operative rehearsal of complex cases or powering
intra-operative guidance systems that monitor for risks and deviations from the optimal surgical plan.

All video generations are performed using the Veo-3 model accessed through the Google Flow platform1 with
the Veo-3.0-quality version. For each sample in the SurgVeo benchmark, the input frame is provided as a
visual prompt, accompanied by the appropriate text prompt (either baseline or stage-aware one, depending on
the experimental condition). The Veo-3 model generates 8-second continuation videos at its default resolution
and frame rate settings. No additional fine-tuning or domain-specific adaptation is applied to the model,
ensuring that our evaluation reflects the zero-shot surgical prediction capabilities of the state-of-the-art video
generation model.

Evaluation Focus:Assessment of whether the predicted surgical operations, as displayed from the input frame
up to the current time point (e.g., 1-second, 3-second, or 8-second), demonstrate appropriate surgical intent
and strategic reasoning for the current procedure. This evaluates whether the overall purpose, goal, and
cumulative surgical effect of the predicted actions are consistent with logical surgical progression, appropriate
procedural steps, and sound clinical decision-making when compared to the reference video.

To foster further research and enable rigorous comparison of future models, the complete SurgVeo benchmark
will be publicly released athttps://github.com/franciszchen/SurgVeo. The release includes:
•All input frames and real surgical continuation videos
•Generated video outputs from Veo-3 for each benchmark sample
•Anonymized expert evaluation scores across all four assessment dimensions
•Detailed evaluation protocols and scoring guidelines

scope.time_horizon: Future observations assessed at 1, 3 and 8 seconds

capability_assessments.rationale: Future-observation prediction is evaluated and retained as positive feature evidence. Under the ontology's implemented core-identity guard, persistent state and an operative learned health-world transition are insufficiently documented for a verified WM capability label. This is not a not_world_model conclusion. The legacy L1 functional summary remains historical; L2–L4 are not demonstrated.

scope.participant_roles: Two board-certified laparoscopic surgeons and two board-certified neurosurgeons.
scope.task: Independent reference-assisted SPP ratings at 1, 3 and 8 seconds.
scope.endpoint: Expert plausibility assessment, not patient benefit.
scope.other_facets: R2/R3 not established: no stated held-out actual-clinical validation design or independent externality. R5–R8 not reported.

gate_assessments.rationale: Provenance and query/reference separation are partial. Availability, pretraining exposure, overlap and complete leakage audits are missing. This prevents pass without proving leakage.
Future-observation evaluation is present, but implemented persistent state and complete transition semantics remain unresolved.
Maximum duration and temporal plausibility profiles are reported. Recursive/block semantics, acceptance tolerance and supported effective horizon are not.
No probabilistic guarantee or uncertainty-dependent decision is claimed for the scoped audit. Uncertainty features remain unreported, not established absent.
The tested queries supply current context, not settable surgical actions/regimes.
No intervention-effect output or therapeutic contrast is produced. This does not validate broader author claims about causal understanding.
No model-coupled optimizer or policy is included in the experiment.
Outputs are assessed offline, not used to change care or physical actions. Privacy/security and future-use risks remain relevant. This is not a safety guarantee.
Procedure subgroup results exist, but independent externality, overlap controls and broader site/population evidence are missing. Different rater pairs confound specialty comparisons.

scope.purpose: Sufficiency of specialist plausibility evaluation for broader assurance claims

gate_assessments.rationale: Actual human participation, the task and results are established and support R4. Broader evaluation sufficiency remains unresolved because rater recruitment/sampling and treatment of reference-dependent valid alternatives are insufficiently reported. Unreported calibration/agreement further limit interpretation. These gaps do not negate human participation or constitute failure of an invented performance threshold.
Live patient/workflow utility is not the tested endpoint. Education, rehearsal and guidance remain proposed applications.
No operational clinical-system release is described. A promised research benchmark is not deployment authorization.

limitations: Automated model review, not independent human verification, clinical adjudication or replication.
This synthesis reviewed all supplied text and all earlier page/image-review notes. Direct page-image inspection belongs to the recorded earlier API calls, not this text-only synthesis.

Earlier page-call statements that other pages were unavailable describe those individual batches. Together, the supplied notes cover physical pages 1–21; they are not evidence that the full supplied synthesis packet lacks those pages.
Source hash, path and page count were supplied, not recomputed. No local files, repository, cited study, underlying video or raw rating data were accessed in this call.
All 128 distinct features have dispositions. Additional track-provenance and model/system E13 scopes do not create independent studies.

Future-observation prediction is evaluated, but persistent state and the operative learned health-world transition are insufficiently specified. Core membership and an ontology-qualified capability label remain unresolved.
Actual reported surgeon participation and outcomes establish R4. Unreported rater calibration, recruitment or agreement do not turn this into simulated feedback or negate human evaluation.

R2 requires a stated held-out actual human/clinical validation design. Public surgical footage and absence of study-specific fine-tuning do not establish it. Readiness facets are not inherited cumulatively.
Fifty clips come from six recordings, not fifty established independent patients. Patient/site counts, eligibility and recording-aware dependence controls are unreported.

All Table 1–2 means and author-labeled SDs are retained. SD aggregation is ambiguous. Zero SD does not establish perfect rater agreement. Confidence intervals and inter-rater reliability are unreported.
Generation repetitions, seeds, retries, failed requests, output selection, generation dates, numerical output cadence/resolution and latency are unreported.
Significant/no-significant wording is not accompanied by reported inferential tests. Prompt effects are descriptively mixed; similar distributions do not establish equivalence.

SPP is a proposed ordinal assessment framework, not a validated hierarchy of model representations or causal capabilities. Instrument appearance and handling overlap, and intent is inferred from visible behavior.
Appendix G.4 specifies cumulative intent assessment to each checkpoint. The same viewing rule is not established for every other dimension.
One reference continuation does not enumerate all clinically valid futures. Reference anchoring and handling of alternative valid continuations are unspecified.
Procedure comparisons also change stages, recordings and specialist rater pairs. Intrinsic specialty difficulty is not isolated.

Figure 6 reports composition of identified errors, not clip-level failure incidence. Raw denominators, counting units, multilabel rules and uncertainty are missing; displayed neurosurgical percentages are not normalized.

Chart-only values are inherited from earlier image-review notes. Static montages cannot independently establish continuous motion, forces, tissue mechanics, surgical intent or representative incidence.
Appendix A describes microscopic cranial procedures, while main methods and prompts identify endoscopic pituitary surgery. Appendix B references Figure 7(a) for both tracks.
Current-public-availability and future-release statements coexist. Repository contents, executable code, weights, licenses and access terms remain unverified.
Plausibility failures and ineffective stage prompting do not establish complete absence of causal knowledge, fundamental reasoning incapacity or the effect of scaling general training data.
No clinical acceptance threshold, effective usable horizon, predictive calibration, intervention-effect estimate, model-coupled surgical policy or prospective clinical benefit is established.

References [1–36] were reviewed as bibliography, not retrieved studies. Unusual metadata and a 2026 EndoChat entry in this 2025 manuscript remain unverified; no capabilities are inherited from citations.

No programmatic schema, semantic-checker or graph validation was executed. The supplied mechanical R4 failure has been addressed with explicit source-linked human-study evidence, but successful checker admission is not claimed.
